elements.locator: A photon of energy E2 − E1 can stimulate an excited atom to emit an identical photon (same frequency, phase, direction).
Gain requires more atoms in the upper level than in the lower level: a population inversion.
Energy-level diagram: pump → upper level → lasing transition → lower level.
Two mirrors face each other around the gain medium; one is partly transmitting (output coupler).
Only light travelling along the axis passes the gain medium many times and is amplified.
Optical pumping: flash lamps or laser diodes excite the gain medium.
Electrical pumping: a gas discharge (CO₂, He-Ne) or a current through a semiconductor junction.
Plane-parallel mirrors are very sensitive to tilt; light walks off the axis.
Stability condition: 0 ≤ g1·g2 ≤ 1 with g = 1 − L/R.
Confocal resonator: R1 = R2 = L.
Divider slide: Properties of laser light.
elements.note: Title or chapter divider; no learning content.

elements.locator: Monochromatic: a very narrow range of wavelengths.
Directional: a small divergence angle.
Bright: high power per area and solid angle.
Coherent: a fixed phase relation in time and space.
Power density I = P / A (W/m²).
A 1 W laser focused to a 100 µm spot gives about 1.3×10⁸ W/m²; a 100 W lamp spreads its light over the whole room.
Linewidth Δλ (or Δν) measures how monochromatic a source is.
A narrow linewidth gives a long coherence length: Lc ≈ λ²/Δλ.
Divider slide: Coherence.
elements.note: Title or chapter divider; no learning content.

elements.locator: E(x, t) = E0 cos(kx − ωt + φ), k = 2π/λ, ω = 2πν.
Two waves interfere constructively when their phases agree.
Temporal coherence: phase correlation along the beam, set by the linewidth (coherence length).
Spatial coherence: phase correlation across the beam, set by the source size.
Lc = c/Δν ≈ λ²/Δλ.
He-Ne laser, Δν ≈ 1.5 GHz → Lc ≈ 0.2 m; white light Lc ≈ 1 µm.
Interference fringes vanish when the path difference exceeds the coherence length.
Mach–Zehnder interferometer: split, delay one arm, recombine.
Fringe visibility drops as the delay approaches the coherence length.
Coherence width w ≈ λ·D/s for a source of size s seen from distance D.
A narrow band-pass filter lengthens the coherence length; a pinhole increases spatial coherence.
Both throw away light, so intensity drops.
Divider slide: Laser output: pulses and beam modes.

elements.locator: CW lasers emit constant power; pulsed lasers concentrate energy into short pulses with high peak power.
Long (µs–ns) pulses melt and vaporise; ultrashort (ps–fs) pulses ablate before heat spreads, leaving little heat-affected zone.
The resonator losses are kept high while the gain medium stores energy, then suddenly switched low.
The stored energy leaves in one short pulse (ns) with high peak power.
Active: acousto-optic or electro-optic modulators switched by a signal.
Passive: a saturable absorber that becomes transparent at high intensity.
TEM₀₀ is the fundamental transverse mode: a single bright spot with a Gaussian profile.
I(r) = I0·exp(−2r²/w²); w beam radius at 1/e² intensity.
Far-field half-angle divergence θ ≈ λ/(π·w0).
Divider slide: Choosing a laser source.
elements.note: Title or chapter divider; no learning content.

elements.locator: Cutting/welding: CO₂, fibre. Marking: fibre, DPSS. Micromachining: ultrafast, excimer.
Material absorption at the laser wavelength decides the choice.
CO₂ 10.6 µm; Nd:YAG and Yb fibre ≈ 1.06 µm; frequency-doubled 532 nm; excimer 193–351 nm.
Wavelength, average power, pulse energy and duration, repetition rate, beam quality M², pump type.
Example data sheet: flash-lamp Nd:YAG, 1064 nm, 10 ns, 20 Hz, 500 mJ.
Divider slide: Beam expansion and collimation.
elements.note: Title or chapter divider; no learning content.

elements.locator: Two positive lenses separated by f1 + f2; internal focus between them.
A negative lens followed by a positive lens, separated by f2 − |f1|; no internal focus.
Magnification M = f2/|f1|; output diameter D_out = M·D_in.
Divergence is reduced by the same factor: θ_out = θ_in / M.
Focused spot diameter d ≈ 4λf/(πD): a larger input beam D gives a smaller spot.
Divider slide: Beam shaping.
elements.note: Title or chapter divider; no learning content.

elements.locator: Many processes need uniform energy across the spot (e.g. annealing, ablation of large areas).
Refractive shapers (aspheric lenses), diffractive optical elements (DOEs), micro-lens array homogenisers.
Gaussian: peaked centre, soft edges. Top-hat: flat centre, steep edges.
Divider slide: Beam splitting and dichroic optics.
elements.note: Title or chapter divider; no learning content.

elements.locator: Partially reflecting plates or cubes split intensity; polarising cubes split by polarisation; dichroics split by wavelength.
Thin-film interference coatings reflect one wavelength band and transmit another.
Transmission curve with a sharp edge at the cut-off wavelength.
Example slide value: a 45° dichroic reflects 1064 nm and transmits 532 nm at 99 %.
Combining a visible pilot beam with an infrared process beam; separating harmonics after frequency doubling.

elements.locator: Galvanometer mirrors, polygon scanners and XY stages move the spot over the workpiece.
F-theta lens: spot position x = f·θ (linear in scan angle).
It keeps the focus on a flat field.
Measured spot 78 µm vs designed 75.4 µm: a 5.5 % deviation.
Free space: mirrors and lenses, any wavelength, alignment needed. Fibre: flexible, robot-friendly, limited by wavelength and peak power.
Single-mode condition: V = (2πa/λ)·NA < 2.405.
Multimode fibres carry more power but degrade beam quality.

nodes.title: Laser optics for material processing
nodes.objective: Explain how lasers work and how their beams are conditioned and delivered for material processing.

nodes.title: How a laser works
nodes.objective: Explain how stimulated emission, pumping and a resonator produce laser light.

nodes.title: Stimulated emission and population inversion
nodes.objective: Explain why a population inversion is needed for optical gain.

key_points.text: Stimulated emission: an incoming photon triggers an excited atom to emit a second, identical photon.
Optical gain needs a population inversion, N2 > N1.
Lasing uses three- or four-level schemes so the inversion can be maintained by pumping.

supplements.text: In thermal equilibrium the lower level is always more populated, so light is absorbed more than amplified; pumping reverses that balance.

nodes.title: Optical resonator
nodes.objective: Describe how a resonator turns gain into a directional laser beam.

key_points.text: A resonator is a pair of mirrors around the gain medium; the output coupler transmits a fraction of the light.
Repeated passes along the axis select a narrow direction, which makes the beam highly directional.

nodes.title: Pumping methods
nodes.objective: Compare optical, electrical and diode pumping.

key_points.text: Optical pumping uses lamps or diodes; electrical pumping uses a gas discharge or an injection current.
Diode pumping is efficient and compact, which is why diode-pumped solid-state and fibre lasers dominate today.

nodes.title: Curved resonator mirrors
nodes.objective: Explain why curved mirrors make a resonator stable.

key_points.text: Curved mirrors refocus the light each round trip, so small misalignments no longer push the beam out.
0 ≤ g1·g2 ≤ 1, g_i = 1 − L/R_i; L mirror spacing (m), R_i mirror radius of curvature (m).
A confocal resonator (R1 = R2 = L) gives g1·g2 = 0, a stable and alignment-tolerant design.

nodes.title: Properties of laser light
nodes.objective: Describe what makes laser light different from lamp light.

nodes.title: Four key properties of laser light
nodes.objective: List and explain the four key properties of laser light.

key_points.text: Monochromaticity: the emission occupies a very narrow wavelength band.
Directionality: the beam diverges only slightly (milliradians or less).
Brightness: very high power per unit area and per unit solid angle.
Coherence: the waves keep a fixed phase relation in time and across the beam.

nodes.title: Power density: laser vs lamp
nodes.objective: Compare the power density of a laser and a lamp.

key_points.text: I = P/A; P power (W), A illuminated area (m²).
1 W into a 100 µm diameter spot: I = 1 / (π·(50×10⁻⁶)²) ≈ 1.3×10⁸ W/m².

supplements.text: Material processing depends on power density, not on power alone: focusing is what makes a modest laser cut metal.

nodes.title: Spectral linewidth
nodes.objective: Relate spectral linewidth to coherence length.

key_points.text: Linewidth: the width of the emission spectrum, Δλ in wavelength or Δν in frequency.
Coherence length Lc ≈ λ²/Δλ, so a narrower line means a longer coherence length.

nodes.title: Coherence
nodes.objective: Define temporal and spatial coherence and estimate coherence length.

nodes.title: Amplitude, wavelength and phase
nodes.objective: Describe a light wave by amplitude, wavelength and phase.

key_points.text: E = E0 cos(kx − ωt + φ); E0 amplitude, k = 2π/λ wavenumber (rad/m), ω angular frequency (rad/s), φ phase (rad).
Interference depends on the phase difference between waves.

supplements.text: Phase is the position within one cycle; two waves 'in step' add up, two waves half a cycle apart cancel.

nodes.title: Temporal vs spatial coherence
nodes.objective: Distinguish temporal and spatial coherence.

key_points.text: Temporal coherence is correlation along the beam (coherence length); spatial coherence is correlation across it (coherence width).

nodes.title: Coherence length
nodes.objective: Calculate coherence length from linewidth.

key_points.text: Lc = c/Δν ≈ λ²/Δλ; c speed of light, Δν linewidth in Hz.
White light has a coherence length of only about a micrometre.
Fringes are visible only while the path difference is shorter than the coherence length.

nodes.title: Measuring coherence with an interferometer
nodes.objective: Explain how an interferometer measures coherence length.

key_points.text: Split the beam, lengthen one arm, recombine and record fringe visibility.
The delay at which visibility falls off gives the coherence length.

supplements.text: Visibility V = (Imax − Imin)/(Imax + Imin) is the measured quantity.

nodes.title: Spatial coherence width
nodes.objective: Estimate the coherence width of an extended source.

key_points.text: w ≈ λD/s; λ wavelength, D distance to the source, s source size.
Smaller or more distant sources are more spatially coherent.

nodes.title: Improving coherence by filtering
nodes.objective: Explain how filters improve coherence at the cost of power.

key_points.text: Spectral filtering improves temporal coherence; a pinhole improves spatial coherence.
Filtering always reduces the available intensity.

nodes.title: Laser output: pulses and beam modes
nodes.objective: Describe continuous and pulsed output and the Gaussian beam.

nodes.title: CW vs pulsed output
nodes.objective: Compare continuous-wave and pulsed lasers.

key_points.text: CW: constant power. Pulsed: energy concentrated in short pulses with peak power far above the average power.

supplements.text: Peak power ≈ pulse energy / pulse duration; average power = pulse energy × repetition rate.

nodes.title: Pulse duration and material removal
nodes.objective: Explain how pulse duration changes material removal.

key_points.text: Long pulses remove material thermally (melting, recast); ultrashort pulses ablate with a minimal heat-affected zone.

supplements.text: Heat needs time to diffuse; a femtosecond pulse is over before the heat can travel.

nodes.title: Q-switching principle
nodes.objective: Explain how Q-switching produces short, intense pulses.

key_points.text: Hold the cavity quality (Q) low while pumping, then switch it high to release the stored energy.
Q-switched pulses last nanoseconds and reach peak powers of kW to MW.

supplements.text: Like a dam: water (energy) accumulates while the gate is shut and rushes out when it opens.

nodes.title: Q-switching methods
nodes.objective: Compare active and passive Q-switches.

key_points.text: Active Q-switches (acousto-optic, electro-optic) are externally triggered; passive ones use a saturable absorber.
Passive switching is simple and cheap but gives less control of pulse timing.

nodes.title: Transverse modes and the Gaussian beam
nodes.objective: Describe the TEM₀₀ Gaussian beam and its divergence.

key_points.text: TEM₀₀: the lowest transverse mode, a single spot with a Gaussian intensity profile.
I(r) = I0 exp(−2r²/w²); at r = w the intensity is 1/e² ≈ 13.5 % of the peak.
θ ≈ λ/(πw0); θ half-angle divergence (rad), w0 waist radius (m).

nodes.title: Choosing a laser source
nodes.objective: Select a laser type by wavelength, power and application.

nodes.title: Lasers by application
nodes.objective: Match laser types to typical applications.

key_points.text: Cutting and welding use CO₂ or fibre lasers; marking uses fibre or DPSS; micromachining uses ultrafast or excimer lasers.
The material must absorb well at the laser wavelength.

nodes.title: Laser types and wavelengths
nodes.objective: Name typical wavelengths of common lasers.

key_points.text: CO₂ emits 10.6 µm (far infrared).
Nd:YAG and Yb fibre lasers emit near 1.06 µm; frequency doubling gives 532 nm.
Excimer lasers emit in the UV, about 193–351 nm.

nodes.title: Specifying a laser source
nodes.objective: List the parameters needed to specify a laser.

key_points.text: A laser is specified by wavelength, power or pulse energy, pulse duration, repetition rate and beam quality (M²).
Example: a flash-lamp Nd:YAG at 1064 nm with 10 ns, 500 mJ pulses at 20 Hz (10 W average).
M² = 1 is a perfect Gaussian beam; larger values focus less tightly.

nodes.title: Beam expansion and collimation
nodes.objective: Design simple two-lens beam expanders.

nodes.title: Keplerian beam expander
nodes.objective: Describe the Keplerian beam expander.

key_points.text: Two converging lenses spaced f1 + f2 apart; the beam passes through a real focus between them.
The internal focus can ionise air with high-power pulsed lasers.

nodes.title: Galilean beam expander
nodes.objective: Describe the Galilean beam expander.

key_points.text: A diverging lens then a converging lens; spacing f2 − |f1|; no internal focus.
Shorter than a Keplerian expander and safe for high-power pulses.

supplements.text: The negative lens spreads the beam first, so the light never comes to a point.

nodes.title: Expansion ratio and output diameter
nodes.objective: Calculate expansion ratio and output beam size.

key_points.text: M = f2/|f1|; D_out = M·D_in.
θ_out = θ_in/M: expanding a beam reduces its divergence.

supplements.text: Because θ ∝ 1/w0, a larger beam diverges less — the same physics as the Gaussian-beam divergence.
Expanding ×10 makes the beam ten times wider and ten times better collimated.

nodes.title: Beam expander as collimator
nodes.objective: Explain why expanding a beam improves the focused spot.

key_points.text: d ≈ 4λf/(πD); f focal length of the focusing lens, D input beam diameter (1/e²).

supplements.text: Expanding before focusing is the standard way to reach smaller spots.

nodes.title: Beam shaping
nodes.objective: Explain why and how a Gaussian beam is reshaped.

nodes.title: Purpose of beam shaping
nodes.objective: Explain why processes need shaped beams.

key_points.text: Uniform intensity avoids over-processing the centre and under-processing the edge.
Annealing and large-area ablation benefit from a flat-top beam.

nodes.title: Beam-shaping methods and components
nodes.objective: Name common beam-shaping components.

key_points.text: Common shapers: aspheric refractive shapers, diffractive optical elements and micro-lens homogenisers.
Refractive and diffractive shapers need a well-aligned input beam of the design size.

nodes.title: Top-hat vs Gaussian profiles
nodes.objective: Compare top-hat and Gaussian intensity profiles.

key_points.text: A Gaussian beam peaks at the centre; a top-hat beam is flat with steep edges.
Top-hats give uniform processing; Gaussians focus to the smallest spot.
A top-hat only exists near the shaper's design plane; it evolves as it propagates.

nodes.title: Beam splitting and dichroic optics
nodes.objective: Split and combine beams by intensity, polarisation or wavelength.

nodes.title: Beam-splitting methods
nodes.objective: Compare intensity, polarisation and wavelength splitting.

key_points.text: Plate or cube splitters divide intensity; polarising cubes separate s and p; dichroic mirrors separate wavelengths.

nodes.title: Dichroic mirrors
nodes.objective: Explain how a dichroic mirror separates wavelengths.

key_points.text: A dichroic mirror uses thin-film interference to reflect one band and transmit another.
Its spectrum has a sharp edge at the cut-off wavelength.
A 45° dichroic can reflect 1064 nm while transmitting 532 nm.

nodes.title: Dichroic mirror applications
nodes.objective: Give applications of dichroic mirrors in laser systems.

key_points.text: A dichroic overlays a red pilot laser on an invisible infrared beam for alignment.
After frequency doubling, a dichroic separates 532 nm from the remaining 1064 nm.

nodes.title: Beam scanning and delivery
nodes.objective: Scan the beam over the work and deliver it by free space or fibre.

nodes.title: Beam-scanning devices
nodes.objective: Name the main beam-scanning devices.

key_points.text: Galvo mirrors are fast and agile; polygon scanners are fastest along lines; stages move the part instead of the beam.

nodes.title: Galvo scanner with F-theta lens
nodes.objective: Explain why an F-theta lens is used after galvo mirrors.

key_points.text: x = f·θ; x spot position (m), f focal length (m), θ scan angle (rad).
The F-theta lens gives a flat focal field and a position linear in angle.
A measured 78 µm spot against a designed 75.4 µm spot differs by about 3.4 %.

nodes.title: Free-space vs fibre delivery
nodes.objective: Compare free-space and fibre beam delivery.

key_points.text: Free-space delivery works for any wavelength but needs alignment; fibre delivery is flexible but limited in wavelength and peak power.

nodes.title: Fibre modes and single-mode output
nodes.objective: Explain when a fibre delivers a single mode.

key_points.text: V = (2πa/λ)·NA < 2.405 for single-mode guidance; a core radius, NA numerical aperture.
Single-mode fibres preserve a Gaussian beam; multimode fibres carry more power with worse beam quality.

supplements.text: A single-mode fibre output is close to TEM₀₀, so it focuses like the Gaussian beam above.
